1:
Calvin explains why the appeal stands here and not at the letter's opening. In case the Corinthians retained any offence at the severity of the previous Epistle, which might stand in the way of his authority, Paul has until now endeavoured to conciliate their affections; only after clearing away all occasion of offence does he recommend to them the brethren at Jerusalem. He could not have attempted it with advantage at the outset, and so deferred it until he had prepared their minds. Henry turns to the phrase Paul chooses, the grace of God bestowed on the churches — though some think it should be rendered the gift of God given in or by them. Henry takes it of their charitable gifts, called grace either because they were very large or because their charity proceeded from God as its author — grace being the root and fountain of all the good that is in us or done by us. Ellicott would modernise the opening verb, there being no reason to retain a phrase now obsolete, and finds it intensely characteristic that the Apostle traces the Macedonians' generosity to its true source.

What the Macedonians gave out of occupies the next three. Barnes notes what makes the gift remarkable: it came when it might be supposed they were unable to give, when many would think they themselves needed aid, and when their minds might have been engrossed with their own concerns — the trial being doubtless a persecution excited against them, probably by the Jews. Their joy, arising from the hopes and promises of the gospel, could not be repressed by it, and they cheerfully contributed largely to the aid of others. Ellicott admits we do not know what affliction is meant, but a community of Christians in a heathen city was always exposed to trials of the kind, and the temper shown by the rulers at Philippi and the Jews of Thessalonica makes at least a petty persecution almost certain. He offers two causes for the poverty. That at Philippi may be connected with the preponderance of women there, since without the bread-winners of a household Christian women in a Graeco-Roman city would find scanty subsistence; and in part the churches shared a widespread distress, Macedonia and Achaia having never recovered from the civil wars, so that under Tiberius they petitioned for a diminution of their burdens. Robertson adds from a historian that the Romans had lacerated Macedonia.

The paradox of the poor relieving the poorer is where the older expositors settle. Clarke states it as a rule: we can scarcely speak of poverty and affliction in an absolute sense, since they are only comparative, so that even the poor are called to relieve those poorer than themselves, and the afflicted to comfort those more afflicted — a duty the Macedonians felt, and so came forward to the uttermost of their power. Gill draws the comparison the other way: for persons in prosperity to be liberal is no great matter, but for persons in adversity, under trying dispensations of providence, to communicate generously to the relief of others is very remarkable, and worthy of imitation. Calvin accounts for it by the joy the verse names. While tried with adversity they did not cease to rejoice in the Lord; nay, this disposition rose so high as to swallow up sorrow, for the minds of the Macedonians, otherwise straitened, required to be set free that they might liberally furnish aid to the brethren. By joy he means the spiritual consolation by which believers are sustained under affliction, and distinguishes it from its counterfeits: the wicked either delude themselves with empty consolations, avoiding a perception of the evil, or else wholly give way to grief, whereas believers seek occasions of joy in the affliction itself. Wesley describes the affliction in three words: continually persecuted, harassed and plundered.
3:
That they gave beyond their power is the phrase the commentators dwell on. Barnes takes it to mean beyond what could have been expected, or beyond what would have been thought possible in their condition, the sense being that they were willing to give more than they were well able; and he notes that Paul, having founded those churches and spent much time with them, was well qualified to bear testimony about their state. He passes on Doddridge's remark that this is a noble hyperbole, similar to that used by Demosthenes when he says he had performed all, even with an industry beyond his power. Robertson supplies the preposition's force, alongside or past their ability, and observes that Field quotes Josephus for the same pair of expressions; few, he adds, give even according to actual ability, and Paul commends this high-pressure collection because of the emergency. Clarke states the same thing morally: in their liberality they had no rule but their ability, believing themselves bound to contribute all they could, and even this rule they transgressed, depriving themselves for a time of the necessaries of life in order to give to others who were destitute even of necessaries.

The next verse reverses the usual direction of an appeal, and the witnesses make the most of it. Ellicott points out that the words rendered "that we would receive" are not in the Greek at all, which runs literally, asking of us the grace, or favour, and fellowship in the ministry of the saints — that is, asking to be allowed to share in it. Robertson takes the same construction, noting that the accusative after the verb of begging is unusual, and that by grace Paul means the privilege of giving: apparently he had been reluctant to press the Macedonians because of their manifest poverty, and they demanded the right to have a share. Clarke puts it plainly, that the apostles had not to solicit them to this great act of kindness, since they even entreated to have their bounty accepted and the administration of it taken off their hands. Wesley supposes Paul had lovingly admonished them not to give beyond their power, which is what they were entreating against. Calvin turns the whole into the argument the chapter is making: if the Macedonians, without needing to be besought, press forward of their own accord, and go further and anticipate others by using entreaties, the Corinthians have something to be ashamed of.

What accounts for the giving is stated in the next verse, and Robertson puts it most compactly: themselves they gave first, and that is the explanation of the generous giving. Barnes fills it out — they made an entire consecration of themselves and all they had to the Lord, keeping nothing back; and he draws the inference for his own readers, that where a people honestly devote themselves to God they will find no difficulty in having the means to contribute. Gill notes that all this was unexpected by the apostles, who knew their great affliction and deep poverty and could not have hoped for such a collection from them. Ellicott adds the second half of the surrender, that they gave not their money only but themselves, their time, thought and energy, primarily to Christ as their Lord and then to the Apostle as his minister — and that they did so because they allowed the will of God to work upon their will. On the sending of Titus, Ellicott reconstructs the sequence: when Titus came to Corinth he had begun to take measures for the collection and had been to a certain extent successful, and it was the report of that success which encouraged Paul to entreat him to return and bring the good work to its completion.
7:
That the appeal opens with compliments is noticed by all, and treated as deliberate. Chrysostom hears the exhortation accompanied with commendations, greater than before; and he marks the verb, since the Apostle said not that ye give, but that ye abound — in faith, meaning of the gifts; in utterance, the word of wisdom; in knowledge, of the doctrines; and in all earnestness, to the attaining of all other virtue. For this reason, he says, Paul began with those praises, that advancing forward he might draw them on to the same diligence here, and of the verse that follows he adds that the Apostle constantly humours them, avoiding offensiveness. Henry calls it great address and much holy art: when Paul would persuade them to this good thing, he commends them for the other good things found in them — most people loving to be complimented, especially when we ask a gift of them, and it being a justice we owe to those in whom God's grace shines. Robertson makes the same observation with an edge: this gifted church had fallen behind in the grace of giving, and there is kindly irony in the allusion.

The list of graces is then glossed item by item. Barnes observes that Paul never hesitated to commend Christians where it could be done with truth, and makes their eminence in some duties the ground of an exhortation to abound in all — from those with so many marks of true religion he had a right to expect much. He takes faith for the full belief of the gospel's truth and obligation, utterance for the ability to instruct others, perhaps their power of speaking foreign languages, and knowledge for the knowledge of God. Clarke runs through the same list: faith is crediting the whole testimony of God, utterance is doctrine, the knowing what to teach, knowledge is of God's will with prudence to direct them in it, diligence is to amend what is wrong among them — so that they should be as eminent for charity as for the rest. Ellicott notes the transition the particle marks, from narrative to exhortation, and how dexterously the Apostle combines the gifts of utterance and knowledge acknowledged earlier with the earnestness and love spoken of in this letter. On the last item he prefers the received reading, your love to us, against the manuscripts giving our love for you, and finds a subtle delicacy in the Greek — the love which, flowing from them, rests in the Apostle.

The disclaimer that follows is read two ways, and Ellicott states the ambiguity: the English, and indeed the Greek, leaves us uncertain whether Paul disclaims merely the tone of command or the sanction of a divine authority. The former seems preferable, though ultimately the one runs into the other, since he gives no commands here because he has received no commandment from the Lord himself. Calvin takes the second horn. Should any ask whether it was not lawful for the Apostle to prescribe what he had by commandment of the Lord, the answer is easy: God everywhere charges us to help our brethren's necessities, but nowhere specifies the sum, nor binds us to circumstances of times or persons, calling us instead to take the rule of love as our guide. Gill states what the refusal amounts to in practice: Paul did not speak peremptorily, extorting a collection or laying his apostolical injunctions upon them, since men in such cases must act willingly, of their own accord and with cheerfulness, not through constraint or grudgingly. Robertson adds what the giving is for: the participle means testing and so proving, and the word rendered sincerity is an old adjective for what is legitimately born rather than spurious — a collection being a test of one's love for Christ, not the only test, but a real one.
9:
Clarke calls this the strongest argument of all, and urged home with admirable address: they are acquainted with God's ineffable love in sending Jesus Christ into the world, and they know the grace, the infinite benevolence, of Christ himself. Barnes explains why the Apostle reaches for it here: Paul was accustomed to illustrate every subject and enforce every duty, wherever it could be done, by a reference to the life and sufferings of the Lord Jesus. The design of the verse is to show the duty of giving liberally from the fact that Christ was willing to become poor in order to benefit others — he who was Lord and Proprietor of the universe being willing to leave his exalted station in the bosom of the Father, that we might become rich in the blessings of the gospel and as heirs of all things. Gill calls it a new argument and a very forcible one, taken from the grace and love of Christ displayed in his humiliation, and adds that his hearers cannot be ignorant of it, there being such glaring proofs in his incarnation, sufferings and death as leave no room to doubt. Wesley states the connection between the two in a clause: this knowledge is the true source of love.

What the riches and the poverty consist in is then set out. Ellicott notes first that the sense of the word grace is slightly modified by the context, the theological sense falling into the background and that of an act of liberality becoming prominent. He would render the participle being rich rather than though he was rich, and finds the thought the same as in the Philippian hymn, especially in the words which ought to be translated He emptied Himself: he was rich in the ineffable glory of the divine attributes, and these he renounced for a time in the mystery of the Incarnation, taking our nature in all its poverty. That is doubtless the chief thought, Ellicott says, but we can scarcely doubt that the words refer also to the outward aspect of our Lord's life, since he chose the lot of the poor. Clarke fills out both terms concretely — he was possessor, as he was creator, of the heavens and the earth, and for their sakes emptied himself, made himself of no reputation, took the form of a servant and humbled himself unto death, even the death of the cross, that through his poverty they might regain their forfeited inheritance and be enriched with every grace of his Spirit. Robertson marks the tenses: the participle is concessive, and both verbs of becoming are ingressive aorists, the poverty being instrumental, the means by which the enriching came.

Calvin presses the argument in two directions. He first establishes the wealth: Christ was rich because he was God, under whose power and authority all things are, and further, even in the human nature he put on, he was heir of all, inasmuch as he was placed by his Father over all creatures and all things were placed under his feet. He then notices what the Apostle does not do. Having adduced Christ as an all-perfect and singular pattern of love — though he was rich, he resigned the possession of all blessings, that he might enrich us by his poverty — Paul does not afterwards state for what purpose he mentions it, but leaves the application to be considered by his readers; for no one can fail to perceive that we are by this example stirred up not to spare ourselves when help is to be afforded to our brethren. Barnes draws the same inference explicitly, that we who are thus benefited, and who have such an example before us, should be willing to give. Wesley defines the wealth that comes of it in five words, that it is riches in the favour and image of God.
10:
That Paul offers advice rather than an order is pressed again, and its wisdom noted. Gill observes that the Apostle did not choose to use his apostolical authority, or to give orders, as he sometimes did, but looked on this as the most prudential step and wisest method to succeed — only to give his judgment on what would be best for them. Robertson calls the word a deliberate opinion and not a command, and Ellicott notes the same careful distinction between command and counsel that appears in the earlier letter. Barnes states the reason it works: advice will go much farther than commands on the subject of charities. On the word rendered expedient he explains that it means this will be of advantage to them, profitable and becoming, since a regard to consistency and to their own welfare bound them to perform what they had purposed. Calvin sets expediency against commandment and admits that the judgment of the flesh will not follow him here — for where is the man to be found who is persuaded that it is expedient to deprive himself of something with a view to helping others? He answers with a saying of a heathen poet, that what you have given away is the only riches you will always have.

The clause about beginning before looks at first like an anti-climax, since the willing is named after the doing, and the two who notice it resolve it differently. Ellicott renders it that the Corinthians got the start, last year, not only as to the doing but also as to the willing, and explains that the order is not a descent but a scoring of two points: they had been before the Macedonian churches in both stages, having formed the purpose of giving and begun to lay by and collect before their rivals had started — so that the Apostle, as a bystander watching that game of honourable competition, gives them a word of encouragement. Clarke takes the difficulty by the word itself. Literally it is to do and to will; but since the will must come before the deed, the second word must here be taken in the sense of delight, as it frequently means in both Testaments — and he notes besides that some manuscripts transpose the words, in which case there is no difficulty at all. Robertson simply reports what the two articular infinitives amount to, that the Corinthians promised before any others did.

Henry states the danger of stopping at the purpose. Good purposes are like buds and blossoms, pleasant to behold, and giving hopes of good fruit, but they are lost and signify nothing without good deeds; good beginnings are well, but we lose the benefit unless there is perseverance. He guards the point on both sides: when men purpose what is good, and endeavour according to their ability to perform, God will not reject them for what it is not in their power to do — yet this scripture will not justify those who think good meanings enough, or the mere profession of a willing mind. Calvin suspects the ardour of the Corinthians had quickly cooled, since otherwise they would without delay have prosecuted their purpose; yet the Apostle, as though no fault had yet been committed, gently admonishes them to complete what had been well begun. On the qualifying phrase Calvin sees an objection anticipated, for the flesh is always ingenious in finding out subterfuges: some plead that they have families which it were inhuman to neglect, and others, on the ground that they cannot give much, make that a pretext for entire exemption. Clarke answers the same excuse in a sentence — give as God has enabled you and as God has disposed you, since he requires each man to do as he can, and accepts the will where the means are wanting to perform the deed.
12:
The measure of an acceptable gift is the disposition behind it. Barnes states the rule at its widest: if there is a readiness, a disposition to give, if the heart is in it, the offering will be acceptable to God whether one is able to give much or little — no donation, however large, can be acceptable where a willing mind does not exist, and none, however small, can be otherwise than acceptable where it is found. Barnes adds that though Paul used it of almsgiving, the principle applies to everything in the way of duty, a willing mind being what God chiefly desires, and that without which all else is offensive and vain. Gill says the same from the other end: if what is done springs from a truly noble, generous spirit, and is given cheerfully and freely and according to a man's ability, the quantity matters not, whether it be more or less. Ellicott notes that the Apostle is expecting a sum large relatively and not absolutely, and suspects behind the words the history of the widow's mite, found in the Gospel of his friend St. Luke, which was probably not unknown to him as belonging to the words of the Lord Jesus which he freely cites — at all events, he has imbibed the spirit of its teaching.

What a man has is then defined, and defined narrowly. Clarke takes it of a man's real property, which means not taking that which belongs to his own family and is indispensably necessary for their support, and not taking that which belongs to others, namely what he owes to any man. Robertson makes the same point from the grammar, that the second clause has a present indicative rather than a subjunctive because a specific case is in view, and draws the plain conclusion that God does not expect us to give what we do not have. Wesley extends the measure well beyond almsgiving. Every believer is accepted with God according to what he hath, and the same rule holds universally: whoever acknowledges himself to be a vile, guilty sinner, and in consequence of that acknowledgment flies for refuge to the wounds of a crucified Saviour and relies on his merits alone for salvation, may in every circumstance of life apply this indulgent declaration to himself.

The disclaimer that follows is read by Ellicott as an answer to something that had actually been said, since the argument that charity begins at home, with which workers in the cause of missions and other distant works of charity are but too familiar, would seem not to have been unknown in the Church of Corinth. Barnes gives the literal sense — not that there should be rest, a remission, to others, but affliction to you — and supposes the Corinthians able to contribute more than many other churches, certainly more than those of Macedonia, so that Paul presses on them the duty of giving according to their means while by no means intending the entire burden to fall on them. Gill sees the same balance inside the congregation as well as between churches, since the Apostle would not have the whole weight of the collection laid on some while others were excused doing little or nothing. Calvin takes the verse as a confirmation of what precedes, that a readiness of will is well-pleasing to God alike in poverty and in wealth, inasmuch as God does not mean that we should be reduced to straits in order that others may be at ease through our liberality. He adds the qualification a theologian would want: we owe to God not merely a part but all that we are and have, yet in his kindness he spares us thus far, being satisfied with the participation the Apostle here describes — an abatement from the rigour of law.
14:
The equality proposed is read first as a reciprocity that circumstances may one day reverse. Barnes points out that Corinth could then give liberally while many other churches could not, being poor and persecuted; but there might be great reverses, Corinth reduced from its affluence and itself dependent on others — so that the church there should so act in prosperity that others would aid them if reverses came. Clarke turns the thought into a rule of conduct: do to those distressed now as, on a change of circumstances, you would wish them to do to you, since human affairs are so liable to change that rich Corinthians may need the charitable help of others as readily as those Jews, who once had need of nothing, came to depend on Corinthian bounty. Ellicott states it simply: the Church of Jerusalem was at this time suffering from poverty, and a time might come when the relative position of the two would be inverted — in which case the Apostle would plead not less earnestly that Jerusalem should assist Corinth. Robertson notes only that the word for equality is an old one meaning fair or equal, found in the New Testament only here and in one other place.

Whether the equality is of one kind or two is itself disputed. Wesley allows a further meaning beside the temporal: as the bounty of the Corinthians now supplied the wants of their poor brethren in Judea, so the prayers of those brethren might bring down many spiritual blessings on their benefactors, the spiritual wants of the one being supplied and the temporal wants of the other. Calvin knows that reading in a stronger form — that the Gospel had flowed out to Corinth from the Church at Jerusalem, so that in their penury the Jerusalem believers had already enriched the Corinthians spiritually — and rejects it as foreign to Paul's intention. He applies the word instead to the communion of saints: whatever duty is discharged to one member redounds to the advantage of the entire body. Ellicott is the most restrictive, calling it reading too much between the lines to find here the thought the Apostle expresses elsewhere, that the equality lay in the Corinthians giving money and receiving spiritual privileges. Gill keeps to the plainest sense: all Paul meant was an equality in givers and receivers alike, proportioned to their circumstances and stations of life.

The proof text is the gathering of the manna, and the expositors reconstruct how the sharing worked there. Barnes explains that the manna which fell around the camp was gathered every morning by all who were able, and distributed at an omer, about five pints, to each man; some would be more successful than others, some by age or infirmity would collect little, and many, confined to the camp, would collect none — so that those who gathered more than an omer contributed in this way to the wants of the rest. Clarke gives the same account with the domestic detail: every man probably gathered as much as he could, and when he measured it at home by the omer, any surplus went to some other family unable to collect enough, the household being large and the time before the heat of the day too short. Ellicott notes that the quotation follows one reading of the Greek version, and that the work of love was in the Apostle's thoughts like the manna itself — in the long run all would be filled, each according to his necessities. Calvin draws the lesson the manna was given to teach, that men do not live by bread alone but are divinely supported, being nourished so for a time that they might learn to be sustained not by their own industry but by the blessing of God — the manna presenting, as in a mirror, an emblem of our ordinary food.
16:
Why the chapter turns to commending the collectors is explained the same way from two directions. Chrysostom observes that having discoursed of almsgiving the Apostle now discourses also of those who are to receive the money and carry it away, since this was of aid towards the collection and towards increasing the forwardness of the contributors — for he that feels confidence as to him who ministers, and suspects not those who are to be receivers, gives with the fuller bountifulness. Henry describes the same passage as a set of letters credential given to the brethren sent to collect their charity, so that if any should be inquisitive or suspicious concerning them, it might be known who they were and how safely they might be trusted. Gill introduces the list in the same terms: the Apostle now gives an account of the persons employed in making this collection at Corinth, beginning with Titus, the rather because he had already been concerned in setting the good work afoot.

The thanks are given to God rather than to Titus, and the witnesses press the reason. Barnes notes that Paul regarded every right feeling, every pure desire, every inclination to serve God or to benefit a fellow-mortal, as the gift of God, and therefore ascribed the praise to him that Titus was disposed to show an interest in the welfare of the Corinthians. Calvin makes the point serve the argument, since it was of great importance to the embassy that the Corinthians should recognise Titus as having come to them stirred up to it by God; and he draws the general inference, that there are no pious affections which do not proceed from the Spirit of God. Ellicott corrects the tense, which is present rather than past — who putteth, not who put — referring it to what was then passing after Titus's return from Corinth; and on the phrase the same earnest care he explains that no direct comparison is expressed, but that the care meant is the Apostle's own, Titus having shown himself a true son of his spiritual father. Robertson makes the same point in fewer words, that the participle presents God as continually giving. Clarke turns the thanksgiving toward the Corinthians: though the poor Christians in Judea were to have the immediate benefit, God put honour on the givers in making them his instruments in supplying the wants of others — and he who is an almoner to God Almighty is highly honoured indeed.

That Titus needed no persuading is the point of the verse that follows, and it is made carefully. Barnes explains that Titus cheerfully complied, but that the phrase means more than compliance: he was more disposed to go than the Apostle had supposed, more ready to engage in it than Paul was to exhort him, so that he anticipated the request and went voluntarily and without urging. Ellicott finds the words serving a twofold purpose, both to show that Titus was authorised by the Apostle and acting at his request, and to show that he was so eager to go that he did not even need to be requested; and he notes that the tense of he went is what is known as the epistolary aorist, Titus being probably about to start as the bearer of this very letter. Calvin marks the same self-correction in the Apostle's own words, since he first says that Titus had undertaken the business from being exhorted to it by Paul, and then corrects himself by saying that Titus had not been so much influenced by the advice of others as stirred up of his own accord, in accordance with his active disposition. Robertson glosses the comparative as more earnest than ordinarily, and Wesley puts it in a clause: Titus was more forward than to need the exhortation, though he received it well.
18:
Who the unnamed brother was is the chapter's standing puzzle, and no two witnesses close it the same way. Gill reports that some think it was Luke the evangelist, the companion of the Apostle in his travels, and notes that the versions differ even on the pronoun, the Syriac and Ethiopic reading our brother and one copy your brother. Clarke lists the candidates without choosing: some suppose Luke, who wrote a gospel and travelled with Paul; others Silas, others Barnabas, others Mark, and others Apollos — neither ancients nor moderns agreeing, though Luke, John and Mark seem to him to have the most probable opinions in their favour. Whoever it was, Clarke adds, he was sufficiently known to the Corinthians, as the Apostle's manner of speaking shows. Barnes agrees that it is impossible to determine and not material to know, but thinks it remarkable that when Paul mentions the man again later in the letter he again withholds the name. Calvin alone commits himself, and against the majority: it is uncertain who the person was, but Chrysostom prefers to consider it Barnabas, and Calvin agrees with him, because it appears that by the suffrages of the churches Barnabas had been associated with Paul as a companion.

Ellicott examines the strongest of the traditions and finds its foundation weak. The general current of patristic interpretation ran in favour of St. Luke, and is represented, he notes, in the Collect for St. Luke's Day in the English Prayer Book though not in the Roman Breviary; but that tradition rested on the assumption, for which there is no evidence and against which there is a strong balance of probabilities, that Luke was already well known as the writer of a Gospel. Apart from that assumption, he grants, there is still more evidence in favour of the Lucan hypothesis than of any other. Robertson is content to leave the matter open, observing that the brother may be, and probably is, Luke, who may also be the brother of Titus by a common Greek idiom in which the article does duty for a possessive — though the idiom is not necessary, and as a matter of fact we do not know who this brother is. Wesley simply records the ancient view, that the ancients generally supposed it was St. Luke, and takes his praise to be for faithfully dispensing the gospel through all the churches.

The second commendation is that the man had been elected, and the mechanics of the election interest several of them. Clarke and Robertson both derive the verb from the stretching out of the hand, so that it means appointed by a show of hands; Robertson adds that the point is that this brother was chosen by the churches and not by Paul, the word occurring only here and in one place in Acts. Gill draws the same conclusion at more length, that he was appointed not by a few private persons, nor by a single church only, but by the joint suffrages of several churches. Ellicott takes the word to imply a definite appointment, here by popular election on the part of the Macedonian churches, and observes how this falls in with the use of the first person plural in the later chapters of Acts. Barnes explains why Paul wanted such a man: he had been unwilling to have charge of the contribution alone, and had procured the appointment of someone to undertake it with him. Calvin states what the arrangement was for: it promotes the glory of God and the kindness of the givers, two things so conjoined that the one cannot be given up without the other being proportionally diminished. Clarke notes besides a textual point, that instead of your ready mind almost all the best manuscripts and all the versions read our.
20:
The verb with which the precaution is announced is read two ways. Gill hears an allusion to mariners, who when sensible of danger steer another way to shun a rock; and so the apostles, aware of the censorious spirits of some, and to prevent all suspicion of converting any part of the collection to their own use, sent Titus with it, a man of known probity, and not alone but with another brother appointed by the churches themselves. Calvin takes the word in the same nautical sense, of furling or altering a ship's sails to change her course and avoid rocks lying in her way, and supports it from Plutarch, who uses the verb of tempests of the mind so severe that they will not let a man shift his course or calm his troubled reason. Robertson derives it more plainly, from an old verb meaning to set or to arrange, so that the sense is simply arranging this for ourselves; and he renders the clause that follows literally, lest any one blame us, noting that the verb of blaming occurs only twice in the New Testament.

Why so much care was needed is explained in terms a modern treasurer would recognise. Ellicott says the Apostle gives here the reason he wished men thus appointed to travel with him: he would guard against the suspicion of those too ready to suspect, and his companions were to bear witness that the sums he took up from the churches were what had actually been collected — auditors, practically, of his accounts. Barnes notes that Paul had for this purpose refused the entire management of the funds and secured the appointment of one who had the confidence of all the churches, feeling how dangerous it is for ministers to have much to do with money matters, and how necessary to hold his own character free from suspicion. Clarke calls it prudent caution, that they might not be suspected of having embezzled or misapplied the bounty. Calvin suspects the danger was real and local: there were not wanting, even among the Corinthians, some who would have gone so far as to revile had occasion been allowed them, and the Apostle wished them to know the state of matters that he might shut the mouths of all.

The maxim with which the section closes is treated as a rule of life rather than an occasional remark. Barnes points out that Paul uses the same expression elsewhere, though there of how we treat those who injure us and here of the right use of property, and takes it for a maxim by which he regulated his life: the word rendered providing means foreseeing beforehand, so that we are to make it a matter of previous calculation and settled plan that all our conduct shall be comely and honest. Ellicott adds what an English reader cannot see but a Greek reader would notice at once, that the words are a quotation from the Greek version of Proverbs — a citation he finds interesting as showing that even one taught by the Spirit could yet find guidance for his daily conduct in the written word; and he notes that many of the best manuscripts give the first person, as though Paul were stating the general principle on which he acted. Robertson draws the corollary: it is not enough for one's financial accounts to be honourable as God sees them, but they should be so kept that men can understand them too — a timely warning, since Paul took the utmost pains that no suspicion could attach to him here. Calvin makes the same double requirement a lesson for others, that in doing what is right the opinion of men is not to be disregarded; and Gill gives the ministerial reason, that when ministers have once lost their credit among men their ministry becomes in great measure useless.
22:
A third man is sent, and he too is unnamed. Gill notices that the number itself may be significant, since in sending three the Apostle conformed to the customs of his nation, or at least agreed with the Jewish canon which requires three persons for the distribution of alms. Barnes calls conjecture about the man's identity useless: some have supposed Apollos, others Silas, others Timothy, but there are no means of ascertaining who it was, nor is it material — it was some one in whom Paul had entire confidence, and evidently one who had been his companion and fellow-labourer. Clarke guesses Apollos, and Robertson will go no further than to say that it was a brother in Christ whom Paul had tested and was willing to trust, possibly Tychicus or Apollos, though we do not know. Ellicott makes the fullest case, and for a name none of the others raise: of those connected with St. Paul at this period, Tychicus seems to have the greatest balance of probabilities in his favour, since he went up with Paul to Jerusalem on this very business, and the tone in which the Apostle speaks of him elsewhere exactly agrees with the language used here — the later letters showing him besides to have been among the most trusted couriers of the apostolic church.

Why this brother was now more diligent than before is put down to the Corinthians themselves. Clarke explains that, finding the Apostle has the fullest confidence in their complete reformation and love to him, the man engages in the business with alacrity and exceeds even his former diligence. Calvin gives the same account with more of the psychology: Paul is not afraid of their coming to Corinth proving vain and fruitless, having felt beforehand an assured confidence that the embassy will have a happy issue, so well is he aware of their fidelity and diligence; and the brother had felt more eagerly inclined partly because he saw that the Apostle had a good opinion of the Corinthians, partly because he had been encouraged by Titus, and partly because he saw many distinguished men applying themselves to the same business with united efforts. Only one thing remained, Calvin adds, which was that the Corinthians themselves should not disappoint them. Barnes reads the phrase the same way, as meaning one who will now prove himself much more diligent than ever before.

The closing verse gathers up all three, and its terms repay attention. Barnes observes that the words any do inquire are not in the original, and that the Greek may mean either if any inquire about Titus or if anything is to be said about Titus — the sense being either that some of the faction at Corinth might question his authority, or simply that having commended his companions it seemed proper to say something in his favour too. Ellicott agrees there is no verb in the Greek and that none is needed, since our common phrase, as to Titus, exactly expresses the meaning; and on the second title he notes that the Greek word is apostles, used here as in one or two other places in a lower sense, without the article, for delegates of the churches, as the Twelve were delegates of Christ. Robertson makes the same point and adds the responsibility it carries, that they were sent by the churches and answerable to the churches for the handling of the funds — financial agents, he remarks, please observe. On the last phrase Calvin explains why such men can be called the glory of Christ: as he alone is the glory of believers, so he ought to be glorified by them in return, and all who excel in piety and holiness are his glory because they have nothing but by Christ's gift. Wesley states it in five words, that they were signal instruments of advancing his glory.
24:
The closing appeal is to be made in public, and Ellicott takes the phrase literally, in the face of the churches. In adding it, he says, St. Paul appeals, as he has done throughout the chapter, to that natural love of praise which takes its place as a legitimate, though subordinate, motive for the activity of Christian benevolence: the Corinthians were not to consider only what he and Titus and the two brethren would think of them, since the eyes of the churches were upon them — probably Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea are meant. With a subtle knowledge of human nature, Ellicott adds, the Apostle attacks them on every side, since they have to compete with Macedonia, to show their love for their teacher, and to sustain the character he has given them. Robertson draws the same picture and gives it a sharper edge: a great host is pictured as watching how the Corinthians will treat these duly accredited agents in the collection, and it requires courage, he observes, to stand by such representatives of great causes before stingy saints. Wesley explains in what sense the churches were present at all — by their messengers.

Two things are asked for, and Calvin separates them: see that our brethren behold your love, and take care that it be not in vain that I have boasted of you. He settles a small point of reference along the way, that the pronoun looks not to the poor but to the messengers of whom mention had been made, since the Apostle immediately subjoins that they would not be the only witnesses — a report given by them would travel even to distant churches. Barnes states the first request in practical terms: by a liberal contribution in the cause for which these men have come, furnish the evidence that you love me and the Christian cause, and show that I have not boasted of you in vain; let it now be seen that my boasting was well founded, and that I properly understood your character and your readiness to contribute. Gill fills in the audiences that would learn of it, since the messengers were sent by the churches and would return to them with their report, and the churches of Judea would see the evidence for themselves when the liberality was brought to them. Ellicott identifies the love appealed to as probably their personal regard for the Apostle himself.

Clarke ends by standing back from the whole appeal and assessing it as a piece of persuasion. On the verse itself he is brief: seeing that these are persons every way worthy in themselves, coming on so important an occasion and so highly recommended, receive them affectionately, and let them see that the very high character given of you is not exaggerated, and that you are as ready in every work of charity as I have stated you to be — act in this for your own honour. He then judges the chapter as a whole. This chapter and the one that follows are occupied throughout in exciting the richer followers of Christ to be liberal to the poorer; the obligation of each to be so, the reasons on which that obligation is founded, and the arguments to enforce the obligation drawn from those reasons, are all clearly stated, and most dexterously and forcibly managed. These two chapters, Clarke concludes, afford a perfect model for a Christian minister who is pleading the cause of the poor.
